items.stem: Why does a country need a constitution?
items.answer:  A constitution provides a framework for governance, defines powers and limits of government organs, outlines citizens’ rights and duties, and states the nation’s core values and aspirations, ensuring order and guiding principles.

items.stem: Explain the ‘rulebook’ analogy used for the Constitution.
items.answer:  Just like a game needs rules agreed upon by all players for fairness, a country needs a constitution as a ‘rulebook’ that lays down fundamental laws and principles everyone agrees to follow for orderly governance.

items.stem: How was the Constituent Assembly formed?
items.answer:  It was formed in 1946 with members elected indirectly by the members of the existing Provincial Legislative Assemblies, ensuring representation from various regions and groups across India.

items.stem: What was the role of the Drafting Committee chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar?
items.answer:  The Drafting Committee was responsible for preparing the initial text or draft of the Constitution based on discussions, reports, and principles decided by the Constituent Assembly as a whole.

items.stem: How did India’s freedom struggle influence the values embedded in the Constitution?
items.answer:  The struggle against colonial rule emphasized ideals like freedom, equality, justice, and self- governance. Leaders carried these ideals into the Constituent Assembly, making them core principles of the new nation’s Constitution.

items.stem: Give one example of how India’s civilisational heritage influenced the Constitution.
items.answer:  Principles like tolerance (accepting different views), Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (world is one family), or emphasis on duties (as in Rajadharma) are rooted in India’s heritage and reflected in constitutional values like secularism, fraternity, and Fundamental Duties.

items.stem: Explain the concept of ‘checks and balances’ among the organs of government as outlined in the Constitution.
items.answer:  The Constitution ensures no single organ (legislature, executive, judiciary) becomes too powerful by giving each some oversight over the others, ensuring fairness, responsibility, and accountability in governance.

items.stem: What is the difference between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)?
items.answer:  Fundamental Rights are legally enforceable guarantees to citizens (e.g., equality, freedom) that can be claimed in court. DPSPs are non- enforceable guidelines directing the state to work towards broader socio-economic goals (e.g., welfare, justice).

items.stem: The RBI is the only legal source that prints and distributes paper currency in India. To prevent illegal printing of notes and their misuse, the RBI has introduced many security features. Find out what some of these measures are and discuss them in class.
items.answer:  The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) ensures that paper currency in India is secure and not subject to counterfeiting. To prevent illegal printing of notes and their misuse, the RBI has implemented several security features on currency notes. Some of the key security measures are :

items.stem: What is the ‘barter system’ of exchange? money

options.label: A
options.text: Using precious metals as a standard value

options.label: B
options.text: Exchanging goods and services without

options.label: C
options.text: A government system for collecting taxes

options.label: D
options.text: A method of digital fund transfers

items.answer:  (B) Exchanging goods and services without money The barter system is an old method of exchange where people directly trade goods or services for other goods or services without using a common medium like money, relying on mutual needs.

items.stem: Which of these was NOT commonly used as a commodity for exchange in early barter systems?

options.label: A
options.text: Cowrie shells or special kinds of salt

options.label: B
options.text: Cattle like cows, goats, or sheep

options.label: C
options.text: Seeds, tea, tobacco, or pieces of cloth

options.label: D
options.text: Digital QR codes on mobile phones

items.answer:  (D) Digital QR codes on mobile phones Early barter systems utilized various tangible commodities like shells, salt, cattle, and cloth for exchange. Digital QR codes are a very recent development associated with modern electronic money transfers, not ancient barter.

items.stem: What is the primary problem associated with the ‘double coincidence of wants’ in a barter system?

options.label: A
options.text: Finding someone who wants your exact item

options.label: B
options.text: The goods exchanged are often not durable

options.label: C
options.text: It is difficult to transport large goods

options.label: D
options.text: There is no way to store value

items.answer:  (A) Finding someone who wants your exact item The ‘double coincidence of wants’ is a major challenge in barter. It means both parties in an exchange must have exactly what the other desires and be willing to trade their items.

items.stem: What does ‘money’ primarily function as in an economy?

options.label: A
options.text: A decorative item used in religious events

options.label: B
options.text: A common tool accepted for making payments

options.label: C
options.text: A method for storing agricultural products

options.label: D
options.text: A system for recording historical events

items.answer:  (B) A common tool accepted for making payments Money serves as a common medium of exchange that is universally accepted within an economy for making or receiving payments in return for goods and services, simplifying transactions significantly.

items.stem: On Yap Island in Micronesia, what unique items were used as a form of money? Click Here to Buy book on Amazon CH 11: From Barter to Money

options.label: B
options.text: Brightly colored bird feathers in coils

options.label: C
options.text: Giant discs of rock called Rai stones

options.label: D
options.text: Bundles of dried tobacco leaves

items.answer:  (C) Giant discs of rock called Rai stones The people of Yap Island traditionally used large, circular stone discs, known as Rai stones, as a form of currency. These stones varied in size and value and were important in their economy.

items.stem: How does using money solve the problem of ‘divisibility’ faced in a barter system when exchanging something like an ox for smaller items? units

options.label: A
options.text: Money can be easily divided into smaller

options.label: B
options.text: An ox can be trained to carry money

options.label: C
options.text: Money is heavier and thus more valuable

options.label: D
options.text: An ox can be sold for other animals

items.answer:  (A) Money can be easily divided into smaller units Unlike an indivisible item like a live ox, money can be divided into smaller denominations (e.g., coins, smaller notes). This allows for fair exchange for goods of varying, smaller values without issue.

items.stem: What does the ‘problem of durability’ in a barter system refer to, for example, when using wheat for exchange?

options.label: A
options.text: Wheat is too heavy to carry around often

options.label: B
options.text: Wheat cannot be easily divided into parts

options.label: C
options.text: Wheat may rot or get eaten by pests

options.label: D
options.text: Everyone may not want wheat for trade

items.answer:  (C) Wheat may rot or get eaten by pests Durability refers to an item’s ability to last over time. In barter, using perishable goods like wheat poses a problem because they can spoil, rot, or be consumed by pests if stored for long periods.

items.stem: The Junbeel Mela in Assam is an example of a traditional fair where the _____ system is still practiced.

options.text: coinage

options.label: B
options.text: barter

options.label: C
options.text: digital

options.label: D

items.answer:  (B) barter The Junbeel Mela, an annual socio-cultural fair in Assam, is notable for continuing the tradition of the barter system. People from different communities exchange their local produce and handmade goods directly without using money.

items.stem: The Tevau, used as money on the Solomon Islands, was made from what material?

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

items.answer:  (D) Red feathers from certain native birds Tevau, a traditional form of currency from the Santa Cruz Islands (part of the Solomon Islands), consisted of long coils made from the tiny red feathers of the scarlet honeyeater bird.

items.stem: A farmer needs shoes, a sweater, and medicines but only has an ox to trade. If money exists, how does it simplify this situation compared to barter? everywhere

options.label: A
options.text: The farmer can directly buy items by value

options.label: B
options.text: The farmer must find someone wanting an ox

options.label: C
options.text: The farmer has to exchange ox for grain

options.label: D
options.text: The farmer must carry the heavy ox

items.answer:  (A) The farmer can directly buy items by value With money, the farmer can sell the ox for a sum of money. Then, this money, being a common measure of value and medium of exchange, can be used to buy shoes, a sweater, and medicines separately.

items.stem: What does ‘portability’ mean in the context of items used for exchange?

options.label: A
options.text: The item’s ability to last for long time

options.label: B
options.text: The ease with which an item can be carried

options.label: C
options.text: The item’s capacity to be split into portions

options.label: D
options.text: The item’s acceptance by everyone in trade

items.answer:  (B) The ease with which an item can be carried Portability refers to how easily an object or material can be carried or moved from one place to another. For a medium of exchange, high portability is desirable for convenient transactions over distances.

items.stem: The Junbeel Mela, where barter is still practiced, begins with the Agni Puja, which is the worship of _____.

items.stem: What is a ‘transaction’ in an economic context?

options.label: A
options.text: A discussion about the value of goods

options.label: B
options.text: A piece of business, like buying or selling

options.label: C
options.text: The process of manufacturing new products

options.label: D
options.text: A government regulation on market prices

items.answer:  (B) A piece of business, like buying or selling A transaction refers to an instance of doing business, particularly an act of buying or selling something. It involves an exchange of goods, services, or assets between two or more parties.

items.stem: Which of these is a modern method of monetary transaction that directly transfers money from one bank account to another electronically?

options.label: B
options.text: Cowrie shells used

options.label: C
options.text: UPI (Unified Payments)

items.answer:  (C) UPI (Unified Payments) UPI (Unified Payments Interface) is a modern digital payment system that facilitates instant electronic fund transfers directly between bank accounts using mobile devices, without needing physical cash or cards for transfer.

items.stem: What is a key difference between commodity money (like salt or cattle) and fiat money (like modern paper currency)?

options.label: A
options.text: Commodity has value; fiat has no value

options.label: B
options.text: Commodity has no use; fiat has many

options.label: C
options.text: Commodity has intrinsic; fiat by government

options.label: D
options.text: Commodity is new; fiat is very old

items.answer:  (C) Commodity has intrinsic; fiat by government Commodity money has intrinsic value (value in itself, e.g., salt can be consumed). Fiat money (like modern paper notes) has little to no intrinsic value; its value is derived from government decree and public trust.

items.answer:  (C) Unit of Account (Measure Value) When a book is priced at `100, money is acting as a unit of account. It provides a common denominator to express and compare the value of different goods and services in monetary terms.

items.answer:  (B) A metal made by combining two or more An alloy is a metal created by mixing two or more metallic elements, or a metal with other elements. Alloys are often used for coins to improve durability, reduce cost, or achieve specific appearances.

items.answer:  (B) The side bearing the head or principal design The obverse of a coin is commonly known as the “heads” side. It is the side that usually features the principal design, often a portrait of a ruler or a significant national symbol.

items.stem: The Chalukya dynasty’s coins often featured a Varaha (boar avatar of Vishnu) image on one side and what on the other?

items.answer:  (C) A decorated three-tiered royal parasol Coins of the Chalukya dynasty frequently depicted the Varaha (boar) incarnation of Vishnu on the obverse. The reverse side often featured a decorated three-tiered parasol (umbrella), a symbol of royalty and sovereignty.

items.stem: Why was paper money introduced as an alternative to carrying large numbers of coins? metal

items.answer:  (C) Carrying and storing many coins was difficult As trade and transactions grew, using large quantities of metallic coins became cumbersome due to their weight and volume. Paper money was introduced as a more portable and convenient alternative for higher denominations.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the sole authority controlling the issue of currency in India today. items.stem: Assertion (A) : Money is said to act as a ‘store of value’. Reason (R) : Unlike perishable goods, money can generally be kept for a longer time and used for purchases later. explanation of A. correct explanation of A.

items.stem: Analyse the transition from barter to money. Why was money a necessary invention for economic development?
items.answer:  Barter faced critical limitations : requiring double coincidence of wants, lacking a common value measure, indivisibility, and portability/durability issues. These restricted trade volume and complexity. Money emerged as a solution, acting as a universally accepted medium, measure, store, and standard, overcoming barter’s hurdles and enabling more complex economic activities and growth.

items.stem: Compare and contrast commodity money (like shells or salt) and metallic coinage as forms of early money. What were the advantages of coinage?
items.answer:  Both served as mediums of exchange. Commodity money’s value often derived from utility or rarity but could lack uniformity, divisibility, portability, or durability. Metallic coinage offered better durability, portability (in manageable amounts), potential for standardization (by rulers), divisibility (different denominations), and often had intrinsic value (precious metals), making it more efficient for wider trade.

items.stem: “Money acts as a link between the present and the future.” Analyse this quote by J.M. Keynes using the functions of money.
items.answer:  Money links present and future primarily through its functions as a ‘store of value’ (allowing present earnings to be saved for future spending) and as a ‘standard of deferred payment’ (allowing agreements like loans made today to be settled with money in the future), connecting economic decisions across time.

items.stem: Analyse how the features of ancient Indian coins (metals used, symbols, rulers’ marks) can serve as valuable sources for historians.
items.answer:  Metals indicate technological level and economic status. Symbols (religious, natural, royal) reveal cultural beliefs, ruling dynasties, and regional identities. Rulers’ marks/names establish chronologies and political authority. Find spots of coins (like Roman coins in India) reveal trade networks and economic interaction patterns between regions.

items.stem: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of paper currency compared to metallic coins.
items.answer:  Advantages of paper : More portable/lighter for large values, easier to produce varied denominations. Disadvantages : Less durable than metal, lacks intrinsic value (value based on trust/government backing), potentially easier to counterfeit without security features. Coins are better for small transactions and durability.

items.stem: Analyse the role of a central authority like the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in managing a modern currency system.
items.answer:  The RBI’s role is crucial for stability and trust. It controls the sole right to issue currency, regulates its supply to manage inflation/economy, ensures uniformity and quality of notes/coins, implements security features to prevent counterfeiting, and maintains public confidence in the currency’s value.

items.answer:  The main functions are : medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account (measure of value), and standard of deferred payment.

items.stem: Briefly trace the evolution of money forms according to the timeline.
items.answer:  Money evolved from barter using commodities, to cowrie shells, then metal coinage (various metals), followed by official paper money, and finally to modern digital forms (cards, UPI).

items.stem: How does using money make the farmer’s situation (exchanging an ox for multiple items) easier?
items.answer:  The farmer can sell the ox for money (a common value). He can easily use parts of that money to buy shoes, a sweater, and medicines separately, without needing double coincidence or worrying about divisibility/portability/durability. NODIA

items.stem: Explain the ‘lack of a common standard measure of value’ problem in barter.
items.answer:  In barter, it’s hard to agree on how much of one good is worth another (e.g., how many shoes equal one ox?). Without a common standard, determining fair exchange ratios is difficult.

items.stem: Why is divisibility a challenge in barter? Use the ox example.
items.answer:  Many goods, like a live ox, cannot be easily divided into smaller parts to exchange for items of lesser value (like a sweater), making small transactions difficult or impossible.

items.stem: How does money solve the problem of ‘store of value’ better than perishable goods like wheat?
items.answer:  Money (coins, notes) is generally durable and doesn’t spoil easily. Unlike wheat that rots, money can be saved over long periods and retains its value for future use.

items.stem: Describe how money functions as a ‘medium of exchange’.
items.answer:  Money acts as an intermediary accepted by everyone. Instead of direct barter, you sell what you have for money, then use that money to buy what you need from someone else.

items.stem: Explain money’s function as a ‘unit of account’.
items.answer:  Money provides a common benchmark (like rupees or dollars) to express the price or value of all goods and services, making it easy to compare their worth.

items.stem: How does money serve as a ‘standard of deferred payment’?
items.answer:  Money allows debts and future payments to be specified and settled easily. Contracts can state payment amounts in money terms, facilitating loans and credit transactions over time.

items.stem: What role did rulers play in the early history of coinage?
items.answer:  Rulers typically controlled the minting and issuing of coins within their kingdoms. The coins often bore symbols or images representing the ruler or kingdom, acting as official currency.

items.stem: How did coinage facilitate trade across different regions or kingdoms?
items.answer:  Coins, especially those from powerful rulers or made of precious metals, became accepted across wider areas, providing a common medium of exchange that simplified trade between different kingdoms.

items.stem: What kind of motifs or symbols were commonly found on ancient Indian coins?
items.answer:  Coins featured various symbols, including nature motifs (animals, trees, hills), images of rulers (kings/queens), or deities from different religious traditions.

items.stem: What can the discovery of Roman coins in South India tell historians?
items.answer:  Finding Roman coins indicates significant trade relations existed between South India (like the Chola/Pandya regions) and the Roman Empire, likely involving Indian exports like spices or pearls paid for with Roman currency.

items.stem: Why was paper money introduced? What problem of coinage did it primarily solve?
items.answer:  Paper money was introduced mainly to solve the problem of portability and storage associated with large quantities of heavy metal coins needed for bigger transactions. Paper is lighter and easier to handle.

items.stem: What is the role of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) regarding currency today?
items.answer:  The RBI is India’s central banking authority and has the sole legal right to issue and control the supply of paper currency (rupee notes) in the country. items.stem: Analyse the persistence of barter systems like the Junbeel Mela or clothes-for-utensils exchange in a predominantly monetary economy. What functions might they serve?
items.answer:  These persist perhaps due to cultural tradition (Junbeel Mela maintaining tribal relations), specific economic niches (recycling old clothes), lack of access to cash in some communities, or social aspects (book swaps fostering community). They fulfill specific needs or maintain cultural practices outside the formal monetary system.

items.stem: Evaluate the statement : “The four functions of money (medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value, standard of deferred payment) are interconnected.”
items.answer:  The functions are highly interconnected. To be a good medium of exchange, money must also be accepted as a unit of account (to know the price) and hold its value reasonably well (store of value). Its ability to store value and be a unit of account makes it suitable as a standard for future (deferred) payments.

items.stem: Consider the farmer’s barter problems (Fig.). Analyse how each specific problem (double coincidence, measure of value, divisibility, portability, durability) would be solved by using money.
items.answer:  Money solves : 1) Double coincidence : Sell ox for money, buy items separately. 2) Measure of value : Ox and items have prices in money. 3) Divisibility: Money comes in various denominations. 4) Portability : Money is easier to carry than an ox. 5) Durability : Money doesn’t spoil like wheat, can be stored.

items.stem: Analyse the information provided by the Arthashastra quote regarding the value of a pana and societal values (Question 6, p.244).
items.answer:  If 60 panas/year equals approx. 3kg grain/day, one pana seems quite valuable relative to basic subsistence. A 100 pana fine for failing to help a neighbour, being more than an annual subsistence wage, suggests society placed an extremely high value on mutual help and community responsibility, heavily penalizing its absence.

items.stem: How might the introduction of standardized coinage have impacted the power and administration of ancient rulers?
items.answer:  Standardized coinage enhanced rulers’ power. It allowed easier and more efficient tax collection, facilitated payment to soldiers and officials strengthening administration and army loyalty, projected royal authority through symbols/ images, and helped regulate/promote trade, boosting the kingdom’s economy and the ruler’s resources.

items.stem: Analyse the security features mentioned or implied for paper currency (Question 8, p.245) and digital payments. Why are they necessary?
items.answer:  Security features (watermarks, threads, special inks for paper; encryption, passwords, OTPs for digital) are necessary to prevent counterfeiting (paper) and unauthorized access or fraud (digital). They maintain trust in the currency/payment system, which is essential for its acceptance and smooth functioning in the economy.

items.stem: Considering the trend towards digital money, evaluate potential future challenges or benefits related to financial inclusion and privacy.
items.answer:  Benefits : Potential for greater financial inclusion for those with mobile access, convenience, transparency. Challenges : Digital divide excluding those without technology/literacy, potential for NODIA

items.stem: What term is commonly used in Hindi for a market, especially a weekly or local one?

options.label: A
options.text: Bazaar or Haat

options.label: B
options.text: Mandi or Chowk

options.label: C
options.text: Dukaan or Gali

options.label: D
options.text: Kendra or Sadan

items.answer:  (A) Bazaar or Haat In Hindi, a market is often referred to as a ‘bazaar’. A local or weekly market, particularly in rural or semi-urban areas, is commonly called a ‘haat’.

items.stem: How does an online market primarily differ from a physical market regarding buyer-seller interaction?

options.label: A
options.text: Online markets have much lower prices

options.label: B
options.text: Physical markets offer a wider variety goods

options.label: C
options.text: Buyers and sellers need not meet in person

options.label: D
options.text: Only physical markets use monetary payments

items.answer:  (C) Buyers and sellers need not meet in person In a physical market, buyers and sellers interact directly in person. In an online market, transactions occur remotely through websites or apps, so buyers and sellers do not need to meet physically.

items.stem: If a seller sets the price of guavas too high (e.g., `80/kg when buyers expect much less), what is the likely immediate outcome in the market?

options.label: A
options.text: All guavas will sell out very quickly

options.label: B
options.text: Many buyers may not be willing to buy

options.label: C
options.text: The seller will make a very large profit

options.label: D
options.text: Other sellers will also raise their prices

items.answer:  (B) Many buyers may not be willing to buy If a seller prices a product significantly higher than what buyers perceive as reasonable or are willing to pay, many potential buyers will likely refrain from purchasing, leading to low sales for that seller.

items.stem: In the chain of supply, _____ buy goods in large quantities from producers and sell them to retailers.

options.label: A
options.text: consumers

options.label: B
options.text: distributors

options.label: C
options.text: wholesalers

options.label: D
options.text: advertisers

items.answer:  (C) wholesalers Wholesalers are intermediaries who purchase goods in bulk directly from manufacturers or producers. They sell these goods in smaller quantities to retailers, who in turn sell to end consumers.

items.stem: What are specialized warehouses designed to maintain specific low temperatures for preserving perishable goods like fruits and vegetables called?

options.label: A
options.text: Godowns for all

options.label: B
options.text: Silos types

options.label: C
options.text: Cold storage

options.label: D
options.text: Granaries type

items.answer:  (C) Cold storage Cold storage facilities are specialized warehouses equipped with refrigeration systems to maintain low temperatures. This controlled environment helps preserve perishable items like fruits, vegetables, and dairy products, extending their shelf life.

items.stem: A garment store offers a 50% discount on all woolen sweaters at the end of the winter season. What is the most likely reason for this price reduction strategy used?

options.label: A
options.text: The sweaters have become very low quality

options.label: B
options.text: To clear out seasonal stock for new items

options.label: C
options.text: Wool prices have fallen sharply in market

options.label: D
options.text: The government has ordered price cuts

items.answer:  (B) To clear out seasonal stock for new items Retailers often offer significant discounts on seasonal items like woolen sweaters at the end of winter to clear out the remaining stock. This makes space for new season’s merchandise and minimizes losses on unsold seasonal goods.

items.stem: What is a ‘retailer’ in the market chain?

options.label: A
options.text: Someone who produces goods in large factory

options.label: B
options.text: One who buys goods in bulk from producer

options.label: C
options.text: A shopkeeper selling goods to final consumer

options.label: D
options.text: A person who transports goods between cities

items.answer:  (C) A shopkeeper selling goods to final consumer A retailer is a business or person that sells goods directly to the final consumers for their own use or consumption, rather than for resale. They typically buy from wholesalers or distributors. Click Here to Buy book on Flipkart CH 11: From Barter to Money

items.stem: Krishnappa, the fruit seller using a QR code for payments, finds it very convenient as he doesn’t need to handle change. However, an elderly customer who always pays with cash feels uncomfortable using the digital method and worries about security. (i) Identify one advantage of digital payment (QR code) for Krishnappa. (ii) Identify one concern the elderly customer might have about digital payments. (iii) Evaluate how this scenario illustrates the ongoing evolution of money and potential challenges in adoption.
items.answer:  (i) Convenience is a key advantage – no need to handle physical cash, calculate or carry exact change, and payments go directly to his bank account. (ii) Concerns could include lack of familiarity with the technology, worries about security (data breach, fraud), lack of trust in digital systems, or simply preferring the tangibility of cash. (iii) It shows the shift towards digital money for efficiency and convenience, driven by technology. However, it also highlights challenges like the digital divide (comfort/ access varies by age/tech literacy) and persistent concerns about security and trust that can slow universal adoption of new forms of money.

items.stem: A government decides to introduce a new high- denomination paper currency note. The RBI is tasked with designing it, incorporating advanced security features to prevent counterfeiting, and choosing motifs that reflect national heritage. (i) Why is it the RBI’s responsibility, and not private banks’, to issue currency? (ii) Suggest one possible security feature the RBI might incorporate into the new note. (iii) Evaluate the purpose of including national heritage motifs on currency notes.
items.answer:  (i) The RBI, as the central authority, ensures uniformity, maintains control over money supply (crucial for economic management), and guarantees the currency’s legal tender status and public trust, which private entities couldn’t ensure. (ii) Possible features include watermarks, security threads, micro-printing, latent images, optically variable ink (colour-shifting), intaglio printing (raised feel), or see-through registration devices. (iii) Including heritage motifs (like monuments, cultural scenes) serves to reinforce national identity and pride, educate citizens about their history and culture, and make the currency visually representative of the nation, beyond its purely economic function. wwww.nodia.i  Downloaded from www.pdf.tube
